clue.text: North American native, bear with me that’s powerful one

indicators.note: read as 'full of power', the word before it is filled up with the abbreviation for power

blocks.note: the polite request for patience, meaning pause a moment
P is the abbreviation for power
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone warns that a North American creature is coming, a powerful one, asking you to bear with them.
explanation.walkthrough: WAIT made 'powerful' (full of P) gives WAPIT, and I for one ends WAPITI. The surface makes 'bear' an animal; it is the verb in a request to wait.
explanation.definitionFit: The wapiti is the large North American elk, a deer indigenous to that continent.

clue.text: Egghead on very nice game show

indicators.note: game as an adjective means willing to go along, so these letters are up for being rearranged

blocks.note: the head of egg is its first letter
V is the standard abbreviation for very
the four letters of nice, rearranged

explanation.surface: A brainy contestant appears on a pleasant TV quiz programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Egghead' and 'game show' look like set phrases, but each splits: egg's head, and game as the anagram signal before the definition 'show'.
explanation.definitionFit: To evince is to display or make evident a feeling or quality, so it is a verb synonym of show.

clue.text: Easy as B and C, but not A?

definitions.text: as B and C, but not A?

blocks.note: first meaning: simple, basic

blocks.clueFragment: as B and C, but not A?
blocks.note: second meaning: being a chemical element, as boron and carbon are while A is no element symbol

explanation.surface: Something is as easy as ABC, but without the A.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on 'easy as ABC', but B and C are the chemical symbols for boron and carbon; there is no element A.
explanation.definitionFit: Elementary means simple or rudimentary, and literally relates to chemical elements, which boron and carbon are.

blocks.note: first meaning: an affectionate way to address someone, like 'dear'
second meaning, whimsical: resembling a duck, a score of nothing in cricket

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a pet name is in fact worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batter out without scoring makes a duck, a zero; adding -Y makes an adjective meaning 'like' it, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Ducky is an informal British endearment for a loved one, and the coined adjective means resembling a cricket score of zero.

clue.text: Movement with paws on ground before pet rolls over

indicators.note: a pet rolling over turns itself the other way up, so the word for it is turned back to front

blocks.note: the prefix meaning before
a pet cat

explanation.surface: A dog trick: the animal puts its paws on the ground and then rolls over.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: in the exercise your hands, the 'paws', stay on the floor. Puss is a familiar name for a pet cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A press-up is an exercise where the body is raised and lowered with the hands pressing on the floor.

blocks.note: pro means in favour of, for
rogues are villains

explanation.surface: Racks or storage designed for criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shelves' looks like a plural noun but is the verb: to shelve is to postpone.
explanation.definitionFit: To prorogue is to discontinue a parliamentary session without dissolving it, effectively postponing business as shelving does.

indicators.note: something not right is out of order, so these letters must be put into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A direction to look left rather than right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left, not right' looks like a pair of opposites, but 'not right' is the anagram signal and 'left' is just L.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'or else', the word means otherwise or in that case, the sense of then in 'if not, then'.

clue.text: Mountain runner holds a book up on a European country

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from the bottom, so the words are written backwards
to hold something is to have it inside, so the runner's letters go around

blocks.note: a ski runs over snowy mountain slopes
A plus VOL, short for volume, a book
the article taken as written, placed on (after) the rest

explanation.surface: A mountain athlete carries a book up a hill somewhere in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' suggests an athlete; it is the thing that slides. The reversed book sits inside SKI, and a final A is tacked on.
explanation.definitionFit: Slovakia is a landlocked state in central Europe, formerly the eastern part of Czechoslovakia.

blocks.note: first meaning: urinating, a polite 'going' to the toilet
second meaning: tiny, trivial (pronounced my-NEWT)

explanation.surface: A question of whether someone is leaving within sixty seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' reads as a unit of time (MIN-it) but is the adjective my-NEWT, meaning tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Piddling is informal for passing water, and also means trivially small or insignificant.

blocks.note: whimsically 'tab-by', like a tab, and a tab is a bill or ticket, so 'ticket-y'
a jeer from an audience

explanation.surface: A cat's yowl from a tabby is praised as excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catcall' and 'tabby' set up a cat scene, but tabby is split as tab plus -by, a joke adjective for 'like a tab', i.e. ticket-like.
explanation.definitionFit: Tickety-boo is old-fashioned British slang meaning all right, in good order.

clue.text: Cruciverbalist, old fellow you would punch?

indicators.note: a punch lands inside the other fellow's space, so one item is driven into the middle of another

blocks.note: a pal is a friend, as in 'old pal'
text-speak for you

explanation.surface: Wondering whether you'd hit an ageing crossword setter.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter clues his own name: U inside PAL. Paul is the pseudonym of this puzzle's setter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cruciverbalist is a crossword compiler or enthusiast, and Paul is the pen name of this crossword's setter.

clue.text: Beaten up, black and blue, giant cut and bandaged

indicators.note: cutting something shortens it, so the final letter of the word for giant is lost
a bandage wraps around a wound, so the bruise word goes around the trimmed giant

blocks.note: covered in bruises
giant as an adjective, very big

explanation.surface: A battered, bruised giant has been wounded and bandaged up.
explanation.walkthrough: TALL loses its last letter to TAL, which is wrapped in BRUISED: BRU-TAL-ISED.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutalised means treated with violence, so it is a past-participle synonym of beaten up.

indicators.note: to set type or a puzzle is to arrange it, so the preceding letters are laid out in a new order

blocks.note: all twenty-five letters of these words are the raw material

explanation.surface: The setter calls his creation a genuine word-processing hazard of his own setting.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the anagram and the definition: this very puzzle, numbered 29,500, really is a word-processing challenge that Paul set.
explanation.definitionFit: This puzzle is the newspaper's Saturday prize puzzle, a grid set to process words and a hazard for solvers.

clue.text: Over top of tower in square, awful gale rose

indicators.note: something awful is in a terrible state, so these letters are scrambled
the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter
one piece sits inside the number word
in a down clue being over means placed above, so the scrambled storm comes first

blocks.note: the four letters of gale rearranged
nine is a square number, three times three
the first letter of tower

explanation.surface: A dreadful gale blows over the top of a tower in a town square, and a rose is caught in it.
explanation.walkthrough: T goes into NINE after its first letter, giving NTINE, with the scrambled gale placed over it.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglantine is another name for the sweetbriar, a wild rose with fragrant leaves.

indicators.note: food that is prepared has been worked on and changed, so these letters are made into something new

blocks.note: all eight letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A cook says they made a fruit posset, a creamy dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: A posset is a creamy custard-like pudding, which makes the kitchen surface convincing.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweetsop, also called sugar apple, is a tropical fruit with sweet pulpy flesh.

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the paper word goes into the other letters
splashed about means scattered, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: the word insert with its opening two letters split off as the insertion signal, the rest rearranged
a ream is a quantity of paper, 500 sheets

explanation.surface: A newspaper supplement carries a big splash headline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'insert' must be split into 'in' and 'sert': REAM goes in an anagram of SERT. 'Splashed headline' looks like one phrase but only 'headline' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: In newspapers a streamer is a banner headline running across the full width of a page.

clue.text: Where business done in secret, a lot to renegotiate when confronted by wife

indicators.note: renegotiating a deal reworks its terms, so these letters are reworked
being confronted means having someone in front, so the spouse letter stands at the head

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A deal made in secret must be renegotiated once the wife finds out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'business' sounds commercial but is a euphemism for a trip to the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A water closet is a flushing lavatory, the room where one does one's private business.

clue.text: Figure requiring recuperation, finally is rallying?

indicators.note: finally points at the end, so only the last letter of the preceding word is used

blocks.note: a number
the last letter of recuperation
taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient needing recovery time is finally rallying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rallying' looks like recovering health, matching 'recuperation', but it is long exchanges of shots in a ball game.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis is a racket sport played in rallies, so the question mark marks rallying as a playful definition by example.

blocks.note: first meaning: Anthony ..., British prime minister 1955 to 1957
second meaning: a state of perfect happiness, paradise

explanation.surface: A long-departed prime minister brings bliss.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Eden was a British prime minister in the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: The garden of the Bible's first paradise lends its name to any place or state of perfect happiness.

indicators.note: evacuating something empties it, so only its outer letters are left

blocks.note: a coy way to say someone is using the toilet
spare with its middle emptied out

explanation.surface: Someone at liberty is going spare, frantic, after an evacuation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going spare' is a British idiom for getting furious, which hides the split; 'evacuation' also plays on the toilet joke. The loo is the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the loose has escaped confinement and is at large, free to roam.

clue.text: Philosopher writing up body part I don’t understand?

indicators.note: in a down clue writing upwards runs from the bottom, so the letters are set down backwards

blocks.note: a limb
the puzzled interjection

explanation.surface: A philosopher writes about a part of the body he cannot fathom.
explanation.walkthrough: LEG then EH, the whole written upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Hegel was the German idealist thinker behind the dialectic, a famous philosopher of the 19th century.

clue.text: All but Q to Z is over

blocks.note: the alphabet without its last ten letters runs from A to P

explanation.surface: Everything except the end of the alphabet is finished.
explanation.walkthrough: The alphabet minus Q to Z is 'A to P', read as a single word.
explanation.definitionFit: Atop means on top of, as a preposition meaning above in position.

blocks.note: first meaning: the Saturday prize puzzle
second meaning: a johnny is British slang for a condom, euphemistically what an old-style barber offered

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to this paper's Saturday prize puzzle. A johnny is British slang for a condom, which barbers famously offered as 'something for the weekend, sir?'
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes weekend entertainment, and is also an old British barber's euphemism for condoms.

blocks.note: it in the old sense of sex appeal, abbreviated SA
a common metal

explanation.surface: A shiny metal, and something about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' as sex appeal is an old crossword convention giving SA, which comes before TIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Satin is a smooth lustrous fabric, and a satin finish is a sheen, so it works as an adjective for shiny.

clue.text: Ultimately, snack good to fill hole – meaty one?

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter of the snack word is taken
filling a hole means going inside it, so the letters are placed within the gap word

blocks.note: the last letter of snack
pi, short for pious, means good
a pore is a tiny hole in the skin

explanation.surface: A savoury snack is just the thing to fill a hungry gap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meaty one?' also plays on rhyming slang: a pork pie is a lie, so this is the 'meaty' kind of fib. PI for pious is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A pork pie is a British savoury pastry with a filling of minced pork, a pie containing meat.

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
people who put on, i.e. add

explanation.surface: People who reach fifty runs at cricket, putting on a half-century.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture of runs and fifty is a decoy: runs are ladders in tights.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladder is a vertical run of unravelled stitches in tights or stockings, so the plural noun matches.
